briefOverview: Jesus is revealed in glory and then teaches his disciples about faith, humble service, inclusive cooperation, and the grave danger of causing others to stumble.
summary: Jesus predicts that some present will see the kingdom of God come with power, then is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, appearing with Moses and Elijah as a voice from a cloud declares him the beloved Son to be heard. He commands secrecy until after the resurrection and explains that Elijah has already come as foretold, while the Son of Man must suffer. Descending the mountain, Jesus delivers a boy from a stubborn unclean spirit after the disciples fail, calling for faith and teaching that such cases require prayer and fasting; the child’s father confesses, “I believe; help my unbelief.” Jesus again predicts his death and resurrection, but the disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. When they argue about greatness, Jesus places a child among them and teaches that true greatness is service, and that receiving a child in his name is receiving him and the One who sent him. He forbids sectarianism toward an outsider casting out demons in his name, promising reward even for simple acts done for Christ’s sake. He then warns sternly against causing believers (“little ones”) to stumble and urges radical self-denial against sin, invoking imagery of unquenchable fire and undying worm, concluding with sayings about being “salted with fire” and having salt within themselves, living at peace with one another.
externalContext: Jewish teachers in the Second Temple period expected Elijah to return before the day of the Lord, based on Malachi’s prophecies, which is why the scribes said Elijah must come first. Peter’s offer to make “tabernacles” refers to booths or shelters; the term also evokes the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), a festival involving temporary dwellings. References to “hell” in this passage translate Gehenna, associated with the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, a site that became a symbol for divine judgment. “Every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” reflects Temple practice; offerings were seasoned with salt as a sign of covenant fidelity (Leviticus 2:13). Exorcism and invoking names in deliverance practices were known in the period, but Jesus emphasizes faith and prayer rather than technique. The title “Son of Man” echoes Daniel 7’s vision of a human-like figure given authority by God, reframed here with a path of suffering.
externalReferences: The heavenly voice, “This is my beloved Son,” echoes the declaration at Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:11) and, with the cloud and Moses’ presence, evokes Sinai theophany motifs (Exodus 24:15–18; 34:29–35). Jesus’ statement that Elijah has come alludes to Malachi’s promise (Malachi 3:1; 4:5–6) and fits the Gospel’s earlier account of John the Baptist’s ministry and death (Mark 6:17–29). The repeated refrain about “their worm not dying” and “unquenchable fire” cites Isaiah 66:24 in warning about judgment. The phrase “Son of Man” draws on Daniel 7:13–14, linking Jesus’ authority with his prediction of suffering and vindication.
practicalQuestions: Where do I need to echo the father’s prayer, “I believe; help my unbelief,” and how can I bring that honestly to God in prayer?
How can I practice being “last of all and servant of all” in my relationships and responsibilities this week?
Am I tempted to restrict or disparage others who serve Christ differently from me, and how can I foster cooperative unity instead?
Whom might I be causing to stumble by my words, example, or influence, and what concrete steps would protect these “little ones”?
What habits of prayer (and fasting, if appropriate) can deepen my dependence on God for difficult ministry and personal struggles?
What drastic but wise boundaries do I need to set to cut off sources of sin in my life?
uncertainAreas: How v.1 (“see the kingdom come with power”) is fulfilled (transfiguration, resurrection, or Pentecost); which mountain the transfiguration occurred on; the precise sense in which Elijah “has come” (identification with John the Baptist is implied but not stated here); the textual variant on “prayer and fasting” in v.29; the meaning of “everyone will be salted with fire” (purification, preservation, or judgment); whether “little ones” refers to children specifically or all humble believers; the scope and imagery of Gehenna in Jesus’ warnings.
